title: Assurance of already-received pardon presupposes prior faith and arises from sensing that faith
source_text: XXII. Adde quod fiducia illa de jam impetrata per Christum reconciliatione, & condonatione peccatorum suorum, praesupponit veram fidem in corde praeexistentem. Nec enim quisquam istud legitime sibi persuadere potest, nisi propriam fidem sentiens atque percipiens, sic apud se ratiocinetur; Quicunque credit in Christum vera fide vivaque, remissa sunt ipsi peccata, & juxta Evangelium justus est apud Deum. Atqui talem fidem sentio atque experior. Ergo mihi sunt remissa peccata, & apud Deum justus propter Christum habeor. Unde manifestum est fiduciam qua ista conclusione exprimitur, esse aliquid fidem sequens ac praesupponens, quodque nascitur ex propriae fidei sensu & consideratione. Sed fidei actus proprius & formalis non praesupponit fidem, sed illam constituit; nec est quiddam oriens ex fidei jam existentis sensu, sed in quo ipsa fidei essentia consistat.
pass_a_gloss: Add that that confidence concerning reconciliation already obtained through Christ and the forgiveness of one’s sins presupposes true faith preexisting in the heart. For no one can lawfully persuade himself of that unless, sensing and perceiving his own faith, he reasons thus with himself: Whoever believes in Christ with true and living faith has sins remitted and is just before God according to the Gospel; but I sense and experience such faith; therefore my sins are remitted and I am accounted just before God for Christ’s sake. From which it is plain that the confidence expressed in that conclusion is something following and presupposing faith, and born from the sense and consideration of one’s own faith. But the proper and formal act of faith does not presuppose faith but constitutes it; nor is it something arising from the sense of faith already existing, but that in which the very essence of faith consists.
pass_b_english: Assurance that pardon is already mine reasons from sensed living faith; it follows faith.
Faith’s formal act constitutes faith; it does not arise from reflecting on faith already there.
